title: Data for "Google's Rich Results Test Displays No More Than 102 Objects for One JSON-LD Entity and Accepts an Invalid eventStatus Value": 215 Archived JSON-LD Versions, Test Files and Captures, Scripts, and Manuscript Versions
abstract: This is a dataset. It holds every saved version of the JSON-LD graphs I built for two websites, mykneeguide.com and orthotoc.com, from January 8 to September 20, 2026. It also holds the test files and captures from my study of Google's Rich Results Test, and every numbered version of the paper that reports the study. The paper is "Google's Rich Results Test Displays No More Than 102 Objects per JSON-LD Entity and Accepts an Invalid eventStatus Value: What an AI Model Got Wrong, and the Three Safeguards That Came Out of It." The paper reports 58 full-entry captures and six screenshot readings, made from September 17 to 24, 2026. The controls read on September 24 and 26, 2026 are in Folder 2 as well, each with its prediction sheet and result record. There are four folders. Each has a MANIFEST.csv that lists every file with its SHA-256 checksum. Folder 1 holds 166 files of the My Knee Guide graph, January 8 to September 20, 2026. They are 152 unique versions, 5 duplicate saves, and 9 files that cannot be parsed as saved. Folder 2 holds 263 files: the built test files and their captures, the screenshots, the prediction sheets written before each run, the result records, and six scripts. Folder 3 holds 63 archived versions of the orthotoc.com graph, January 17 to May 13, 2026. With the 152 unique versions in Folder 1 they are the 215 archived JSON-LD versions in the title. Folder 4 holds 106 numbered versions of the manuscript, September 19 to 27, 2026, from the first draft through the version immediately before the submitted manuscript. Any two of them can be compared to see every change between them. The archived JSON-LD files are old versions of the structured data on my websites. They are evidence of how a tool behaved. They are not a description of me. As of September 20, 2026, only one file, MKG Schema 11.9, is the version I stand behind. I will keep updating the graph on mykneeguide.com after this deposit, and the version live on the site at the time is the one I stand behind. The files are deposited byte for byte as they were saved, so the errors in them are still in them. The README carries a correction statement that lists the five statements about me in the archived versions that were wrong when they were written and the version in which each was corrected.The screenshots show Google's Rich Results Test, Google Search Console and the Schema Markup Validator at validator.schema.org. The license covers only what is mine in them.

title: X-Crypt: Amplitude-Based Encryption Derived from ZEUS (Zero-Entropy Unified Substrate), an Emergent Information-Geometric Substrate
abstract: This record contains the preprint X-Crypt: Amplitude-Based Encryption Derived from ZEUS (Zero-Entropy Unified Substrate), an Emergent Information-Geometric Substrate and its Appendix A, the public test passage. The preprint reports foundation measurements on the live state of an X-Crypt instance, evaluated exclusively from recorded amplitude data: bit-exact reproducibility across independent instantiations, rigidity of the fixed point over thousands of iterations, independence of the fixed point from the state history, the factorisation of the fixed point into an input scalar and an instance vector under scalar inputs, instance binding concentrated in the network's bottleneck, shape invariance of the whole network over the transient, and the same behaviour in a second network of different structure. The measurements validate the base assumption of X-Crypt: that the instance-bound amplitude landscape has the properties required of cryptographic material. Appendix A consists of two files. XCrypt_AppendixA_TestPassage2_Cipher.txt is the X-Crypt ciphertext of a short passage of continuous prose: 238 lines, one amplitude per character, spaces included, no sentence markers. Its SHA-256 is 5c96319c985fa603b45c7ceb9ec825225ff14ec955e3ebdefecf1de850220ae0. XCrypt_AppendixA_TestPassage2_Commitment.json seals the plaintext in advance: it contains the SHA-256 and SHA-512 of the exact plaintext, the SHA-256 of the ciphertext file, and the plaintext encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with nonce and ciphertext disclosed and the key withheld. The attack model is the one stated in the paper: the reader holds the ciphertext and the procedure and does not hold the instance, the positional map or the credential. The solving period is six weeks from the publication date of this record. After that period the AES key, the plaintext, the recorded amplitude landscapes of all measurements and the analysis scripts will be released in an updated version of this record, so that the commitment can be verified and every quantity in the paper recomputed. No scripts, constants, weights or descriptions of the generating system are part of the release. Anyone who recovers the plaintext, in whole or in part, feel free to contact me. You can reach me at info@trauth-research.com or via LinkedIn https://www.linkedin.com/in/stefantrauth/. A submission should contain the recovered plaintext or its SHA-256, which can be checked against the hash in the commitment file. Every submission received within the solving period will be acknowledged, and a successful recovery will be reported openly in the updated version of this record. The solution of the test passage — the plaintext, the character-by-character assignment and the positional maps — is deposited in a separate, restricted Zenodo record (10.5281/zenodo.23119682 - https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23119682) as an AES-256-encrypted archive together with the tool that opens it. The record carries the same plaintext hash as stated here and is opened on 8 November 2026, at the end of the six-week solving period, when the passphrase is published and the recorded landscapes and analysis scripts are released in an updated version of this record.

title: Kalyvox Voice Benchmark 2026
abstract: Benchmark dataset measuring AI voice agent performance across 240 controlled test calls covering 12 standardized scenario families in French and English. The benchmark includes 120 French and 120 English calls conducted between August 22 and September 22, 2026. The dataset contains one row per controlled test call, including scenario information, expected and detected intent, response latency, intent correctness, task completion, transfer results, appointment booking results, fallback handling and call duration. Key benchmark results:- Median response latency: 735 ms- P95 response latency: 1,079 ms- Intent accuracy: 94.6%- Task completion: 91.2%- Successful call transfers: 96.7% (58/60)- Successful appointment bookings: 87.5% (35/40)- Correct fallback handling: 91.7% (55/60) Tests were performed using standardized scenarios designed to evaluate common AI receptionist tasks and failure cases. Full methodology, metric definitions and analysis:https://kalyvox.ai/en/ai-voice-agent-benchmark

title: RelaxKV: Recomputation Guided by the Query with Sparse Context Attention for Efficient KV Cache Reuse
abstract: Cross-request KV caching reduces the prefill cost of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), but conventional prefix caching severely limits cache reuse across requests. Position-Independent Caching (PIC) removes this constraint by reusing independent chunks, but their KV states miss cross-chunk interactions. Existing methods selectively recompute token states to recover these missing interactions, but primarily allocate the recomputation budget to selecting which states to recompute, while fixing the recomputation context to the full causal prefix. We introduce RelaxKV, which formulates selective cache repair as a joint allocation problem over repair targets and recomputation context. Guided by the user query, RelaxKV identifies layer-specific repair targets and restricts their recomputation to a query-relevant context, reducing attention computation. Across four decoder models, RelaxKV at a 15% anchor ratio improves aggregate LongBench performance over ProphetKV on all models. On Qwen3-14B, RelaxKV provides a stronger quality-TTFT trade-off than ProphetKV across a 5%-30% anchor-ratio sweep, and achieves the best selective results on RULER-MV and LV-Eval at 16K and 32K context lengths. Controlled ablations further demonstrate the importance of recomputation context selection.

title: The cost of useful natural gradient updates
abstract: What information is needed to turn a natural-gradient direction into a useful finite update? Under a population Kullback-Leibler (KL) budget, we call a step useful if it is feasible and loses at most a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the best feasible gain along the direction. We construct a four-state exponential family whose laws share their initial gradient, scalar Fisher information and natural gradient, yet two laws have disjoint useful-step sets. With these quantities supplied exactly and the law otherwise known only through draws, the family's worst-case sample complexity is $Θ(\log(1/δ)/(p\varepsilon^2))$ for small $\varepsilon$, where $p$ scales rare-state probabilities and $δ$ is the failure probability. The budget is fixed and the optimal gain stays bounded away from zero, so the step length, not the direction, carries this cost. For succinctly described event-tilt models, returning a useful step is NP-hard even with the exact natural gradient and efficient exact sampling. Recovering the unit natural gradient to constant error is also NP-hard even in a two-parameter logistic family with Fisher condition number at most 3. We also give matching sample bounds for event tilts, sample bounds for damped Fisher solves and a population-KL certificate for affine classifiers. In frozen-feature classifier heads, stopping at a sampled KL boundary succeeds in about half of the trials, and a 10% KL margin raises joint success above 93% at a KL budget of 0.01. Thus, knowing where to move is not enough: how far to move can carry an update's entire cost.

title: Post-Quantum Secure Authentication for Constrained Iot Devices Using NTRU Lattice Cryptographic Techniques
abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the suitability of the lattice-based NTRU post-quantum cryptography algorithm for securing Internet of Things (IoT) environments, which face increasing risks from quantum-enabled attacks and require long-term, efficient cryptographic protection resource-constrained IoT devices. The study analyzes the performance, computational demands, and scalability of NTRU within resource-constrained IoT devices. It examines NTRU in comparison with traditional public-key systems such as RSA-2048, considering factors such as key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) efficiency, where KEM refers to secure key exchange through encapsulation and decapsulation, memory usage, and processing overhead. Findings show that NTRU achieves more than 90% faster computation compared to RSA-2048, demonstrating significant improvements in speed and resource efficiency. These characteristics make NTRU a capable option for embedded and low-power IoT devices, where computational and energy constraints are critical. NTRU presents a promising solution for implementing post-quantum authentication in IoT systems. While some optimization challenges remain, its strong performance and suitability for resource-constrained environments position it as a viable candidate for future secure IoT deployments in the post-quantum era.

title: Speech-guided unmanned aerial vehicle control system based on large language model-structured execution graphs with expert rule constraints
abstract: As the use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) expands into industrial and safety-critical applications, there is an increasing need for intuitive speech-driven control systems that reduce reliance on predefined command sets or manual interfaces. Natural language instructions, however, often exhibit ambiguity, logical inconsistency, and a lack of structured representation, which limits their direct applicability to UAV operations. This research develops a speech-guided UAV control system that leverages large language models (LLMs) to construct execution graphs from natural language commands, augmented with expert rule validation for reliable and transparent aerial autonomy. These graphs capture semantically organized control sequences and are refined through expert rule constraints that verify logical consistency, eliminate infeasible actions, and resolve dependency issues. The use of in-context learning enables the LLM to generalize across diverse expressions without requiring additional fine-tuning. The system was evaluated through three experiments targeting language understanding, graph structuring, and rule-based validation. It achieved up to 95.4% accuracy on complex spoken commands, structured 1,000 natural instructions into executable graphs with over 98% accuracy, and corrected all structural issues using expert-defined rules. Real-time performance was maintained with an average latency under two seconds. This work establishes a practical framework for integrating LLMs into voice-controlled UAV systems while ensuring robustness through rule-based validation.

title: École: Privacy in Diversity
abstract: As part of the political process, citizens may participate in (signature) collections to influence policy changes. Depending on the legislative basis, such collections may even result in legally binding acts. Unlike e-voting systems, the security of such collecting systems remains unexplored. In this work, we first derive a realistic setting for e-collecting based on e-voting. Then, we propose the secure protocol École in this setting, achieving both privacy and verifiability under realistic trust assumptions. Notably, participation privacy is guaranteed without the need for an anonymous channel, by assuming that at any given point in time, many diverse collections are active in parallel.

title: NxM-Version Programming for Quantum Software: High-Level Components across Frameworks and Engines
abstract: Quantum computing has in recent years evolved from a purely theoretical field to an active area in both academia and industry. As a result, Quantum Software Engineering has emerged as an area that aims to organize the process of building, testing, and running quantum software. However, writing quantum software still requires programming with quantum gates and qubits, as well as knowledge specific to quantum software frameworks such as Qiskit, Cirq, Qrisp, pyQuil and PennyLane, each of which reaches quantum hardware through its own toolchain. We present Quanifi, which packages the high-level routines of these frameworks as components on the Apache NiFi dataflow canvas. The components exchange circuits as OpenQASM 2.0, so a circuit built by one framework can be executed by another. This allows for two types of redundancy: several frameworks implement the same algorithm, and several engines (simulators or real hardware) execute the same circuit. We describe N$\times$M program execution, which crosses the two: a single NiFi flow runs each of the $N$ implementations on each of the $M$ engines, and because every result is labelled with its implementation and its engine, a disagreement can be linked to an implementation, to an engine, or to a single implementation-engine pair. We ran Grover's algorithm built by three frameworks on three quantum computers from IBM, IQM and Quantum Inspire, and a matrix of three adder builders on one IQM device reached through two routes. N$\times$M execution helped us discover three real defects: an incorrect gate-set declaration in the Quantum Inspire adapter, execution consistent with negated $R_x$ angles on Tuna-17, and circuit modification through Open Quantum. The latter two returned wrong answers without reporting an error. We reported all three defects and Open Quantum's provider confirmed and fixed its QASM parsing defect.

title: VGGT-Diff: Visual Geometry Meets Diffusion for Sparse-View Novel View Synthesis
abstract: We present VGGT-Diff, a geometry-routed multi-view diffusion model for sparse-view novel view synthesis. Existing novel view synthesis (NVS) methods face a fundamental trade-off: reconstruction-based approaches preserve observed geometry but struggle to synthesize unseen regions, while diffusion-based methods provide strong generative priors yet rely on implicit source-to-query correspondence. VGGT-Diff bridges these regimes by routing visual geometry latents from VGGT-Ω into a pretrained video diffusion model. Each visual token is associated with a 3D point and confidence, then transformed into query-aligned latent conditions through a confidence-aware Visual Geometry Router (VGR) that preserves front and back surface evidence. These conditions guide joint target-view denoising, while Point-Track Residual Consistency (PTRC) regularizes predicted-clean residuals along reliable 3D tracks, improving multi-view stability. We further introduce robust geometry conditioning, combining training-time regularization with inference-time guidance for improved robustness. Experiments show competitive or state-of-the-art performance across interpolation and extrapolation under different viewpoint difficulties. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenkangjie1123/VGGT-Diff.

Each visual token is associated with a 3D point and confidence, then transformed into query-aligned latent conditions through a confidence-aware Visual Geometry Router (VGR) that preserves front and back surface evidence. These conditions guide joint target-view denoising, while Point-Track Residual Consistency (PTRC) regularizes predicted-clean residuals along reliable 3D tracks, improving multi-view stability. We further introduce robust geometry conditioning, combining training-time regularization with inference-time guidance for improved robustness. Experiments show competitive or state-of-the-art performance across interpolation and extrapolation under different viewpoint difficulties. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenkangjie1123/VGGT-Diff.

title: Association schemes from vectorial generalized Maiorana-McFarland bent functions with non-weakly regular components
abstract: Let $p$ be an odd prime, $q=p^k$, and $r=p^s$ with $s\mid k$. We study $\mathbb{F}_r$-valued generalized Maiorana-McFarland functions $H(x,y,z)=P^{(z)}(x)+\operatorname{Tr}_s^k(yz)$ on $V_n\times\mathbb{F}_q\times\mathbb{F}_q$. The ingredients $P^{(z)}$ are vectorial dual-bent functions with weakly regular components, constant on the cosets of $\mathbb{F}_r^*$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^*$, and, for $z\ne 0$, of inversion type with respect to $t\mapsto t^{-1}$. Under a mild condition on $P^{(0)}$, we prove that the partition into the $\mathbb{F}_r$-valued level sets of $H$, refined according to the $\mathbb{F}_r$-lines of the relevant coordinates, is Fourier-reflexive. It therefore induces a translation association scheme with $\frac{q-1}{r-1}(r+1)+r$ classes (one fewer in a degenerate case), symmetric when the ingredients are even. For $s=1$ this recovers recent scalar constructions, while for $s=k$ it yields $(2q+1)$-class schemes from vectorial bent functions whose components may all be non-weakly regular. We also construct fusions along $\mathbb{F}_r$-subspaces, obtaining $(2r+1)$- and $(3r+2)$-class schemes and connections between different levels. Counterexamples show that the inversion, coset-constancy, subspace, and weak-regularity hypotheses cannot in general be omitted. To our knowledge, these are the first association schemes obtained from vectorial bent functions with non-weakly regular components.

title: Complementary Transport and Feynman Composition
abstract: Complex multiplication, coherent addition, and quadratic readout are related ingredients of quantum calculation, but they answer different reconstruction questions. We separate them on a supplied reciprocal carrier. The centralizer of a complex structure on a real two-plane is the complex algebra; its invertible transports are nevertheless not closed under the addition needed for destructive interference at a selected output. A one-outcome dephaser and a reversible phase kick show that certainty of a public outcome does not imply nondisturbance. Within an explicitly assumed positive quadratic response class, calibrated zero-leakage comparisons on a connected tree select the all-ones Gram kernel. We prove quantitative stability estimates and retain the distinction between unconditional record-local operations, selective conditioning, and a controlled inverse interaction. A local normalized-weight ansatz, arbitrary anchored orthogonal refinement, and additive coarse-graining of recorded outcomes force weights proportional to quadratic size. Equal binary refinement alone does not: a positive continuous increasing log-periodic function supplies a counterexample, while binary and ternary refinement at every size, with continuity, recover linearity in size. Real rotations implement the requisite refinements and controlled tagging without full complex control. Fixed-complement preservation and reciprocal reversal admit different generator sectors; independently switchable real mixers on a connected graph plus one addressable local phase generate the unitary Lie algebra. A common scalar phase does not. Supplementary finite action–phase and history examples expose the remaining calibration assumptions. The contribution is an assumption-controlled synthesis of conditional selectors and obstructions, not the introduction of the standard component constructions. The carrier, comparison response, control resources, tensor interpretation, and empirical probability interface are not derived from primitive complementarity.

title: The door is the hardest room: entry-level clinical research training reads four grades above every advanced course
abstract: Background. Clinical research capacity strengthening assumes that removing cost and language barriers admits people to the field. Reading level is a third barrier, it is rarely measured, and unlike the other two it is invisible to the organization that creates it: an author cannot feel the difficulty of their own prose. Methods. Flesch-Kincaid grade level, words per sentence and acronym count were computed for every lesson in a free, openly licensed clinical research training corpus: 357 lessons across 11 courses, 274,147 words, measured 27 September 2026. Courses span two audiences: workforce training for coordinators, monitors, investigators and data managers, and plain-language guides written for trial participants. Results. The corpus mean is grade 10.98 (SD 2.90). One course is a severe outlier: fundamentals-of-clinical-research, the designated entry point, reads at grade 16.2 against 11.8 for the next hardest and 8.0 for the participant guides. 84.2 percent of its lessons sit at or above grade 14, against 3.3 percent for the next course and 0 percent for the remaining nine. The gap is not explained by terminology. Acronym density correlates with grade level at r = 0.142 and the entry course has fewer acronyms than four courses that read easier; the GCP course carries 2.7 times as many acronyms and reads 4.4 grades lower. Sentence length correlates at r = 0.848, and the entry course averages 21.5 words per sentence against 13.5 to 17.3 elsewhere. Conclusions. In this corpus, reading difficulty is a property of syntax rather than vocabulary, and the hardest text sits at the point of entry. The direction of the error matters: a platform whose stated purpose is access had made its front door its least accessible room, and no one noticed until it was measured, because difficulty is not visible from the inside. The finding is presented as a measurement of one corpus, not as evidence of harm: this study does not test comprehension and cannot show that grade level changed what anyone learned.

title: DecisionModelBench: Empirical Benchmark of Non-Autoregressive Decision Models vs Foundation LLMs in Cyber-Physical Systems, Algorithmic Trading, and Civic Emergency Triage
abstract: DecisionModelBench is an empirical benchmark platform and scientific research repository evaluating Non-Autoregressive Decision Models (System 1) against Foundation Generative Large Language Models (System 2) across dual NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU distributed topologies. This deposition contains the complete reproducible experimental codebase, multi-GPU sharding pipelines, simulation engines, dataset results, and two foundational scientific research papers authored by Richie O. Sumual (PANITA GORONTALO): Paper 1: The Autoregression Fallacy in Time-Critical Cyber-Physical Systems and Algorithmic Trading: An Empirical Benchmark of Non-Autoregressive Decision Models versus Foundation Large Language Models (English & Indonesian editions, PDF & LaTeX). Paper 2: Deterministic Intent Gating, Sovereign Emergency Calling, and Two-Tier Civic Triage: An Empirical Evaluation of Non-Autoregressive Decision Models versus Foundation Large Language Models in Municipal 911/112 Operations and High-Throughput Public Administration (English & Indonesian editions, PDF & LaTeX). Key Empirical Findings Sub-100 ms Reflex Triage: Compact non-autoregressive models (Laya 421M ModernBERT at 35–55 ms, OpenJev 0.5B at 180–240 ms, TypeSafe JEV at 160 ms) achieve sub-second determinism with 0 output tokens. Autoregression Fallacy Demarcation: Standalone autoregressive LLMs (Sahabat-AI 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 2 9B) incur multi-second memory bandwidth bottlenecks (2,200 ms to 12,680 ms), inducing catastrophic state-decision drift in air defense, -$19.41 P&L slippage in trading, and Erlang-C queue explosions in emergency hotlines. Decoupled Two-Tier Architecture: Demonstrates that decoupling sub-100ms deterministic triage (System 1) from asynchronous conversational deliberation (System 2) resolves statutory SLA violations (<3s in 911/112 dispatch) and saves 80%–100% of GPU compute costs. Portal & Interactive Simulations: https://tuwiliyt.github.io/decisionmodelbench/

title: Evidence, limitations and implications for renewable energy planning of daily global solar irradiation in tropical climate zones of Cameroon, predicted by machine learning
abstract: Accurate solar irradiance prediction is a crucial step for the efficient planning and deployment of solar energy systems, particularly in tropical regions like Cameroon where solar resources remain largely untapped. Despite growing global interest in solar energy prediction using machine learning techniques, this remains a significant challenge. Similar studies exist in Cameroon, but they remain few compared to those in Asia, Europe, or North Africa. In contrast, our study stands out due to its complementary geographic coverage, the inclusion of solar vortex mass (SVM), and the in-depth analysis of predictive meteorological variables (particularly cloud cover). This study aims to help fill this gap by predicting daily global solar irradiance on horizontal surfaces in five Cameroonian cities Bertoua, Douala, Garoua, Maroua, and Yaoundé characterized by relatively diverse climatic conditions. Four machine learning algorithms were used for this purpose: Linear Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine. Meteorological parameters including mean air temperature, relative humidity, precipitation, wind speed, wind direction, day of the year, atmospheric pressure, and cloud cover were used as input variables for training the models. The dataset was obtained from NASA’s POWER database over 27 years and covers the period from 1999 to 2026. Model performance was evaluated using three statistical indicators: mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and coefficient of determination (R 2 ). The results show that RMSE values range from 0.58 to 0.77 kWh/m 2 , MAE values from 0.40 to 0.59 kWh/m 2 , and R 2 values from 0.52 to 0.69, across all cities and models. Among the four algorithms evaluated, the Random Forest model consistently achieved the best predictive performance in all cities, followed by the Support Vector Machine, the Decision Tree model, and the linear model. These results suggest that the Random Forest algorithm is the most suitable model for predicting global daily solar irradiation in Cameroon and can serve as a preliminary selection tool for assessing solar energy resources in the region, while enriching the scientific literature on solar irradiation modeling in Central Africa.

title: An Active-Bottleneck Mechanism for Weak-to-Strong Generalization
abstract: Weak-to-strong generalization (W2SG) occurs when a student trained on a teacher's predictions outperforms that teacher. We study when this happens under fully converged, ridgeless two-stage learning, with no early stopping, no explicit regularization, and no assumption that the student is more expressive than the teacher. In two-stage linear regression, a teacher is fit from $n$ labeled examples and a student is trained solely on the teacher's predictions on $m$ fresh, unlabeled inputs. Although both stages share the same hypothesis class and the same training rule, we show that the student outperforms the teacher exactly when $m$ lies in an explicit intermediate range: too few pseudo-labels leave the student without enough signal, too many let it inherit the teacher's noise. Under power-law covariance, we derive this range in closed form as a function of the spectral decay and noise level, including regimes where the improving region splits into two disjoint intervals of $m$. We then study a random-feature model in which the student has strictly more features than the teacher, and identify two regimes, again given by explicit thresholds: one where improvement occurs only for $m$ in a bounded interval, and one where it occurs only once the student width $N_S$ exceeds an explicit threshold. Both regimes are governed by a single "active-bottleneck" principle: whichever of $m$ or $N_S$ is scarcer controls how much teacher error is filtered out, while increasing the other resource only reduces estimation noise. Together, these results show that finite data and finite width can themselves regularize a two-stage learner, with no explicit mechanism doing so.

title: PackServe: SLO-Aware Request Scheduling for Agentic LLM Serving at Scale
abstract: Request scheduling is a key challenge in large-scale clusters serving agentic large language model (LLM) workloads. An effective scheduler must preserve key-value cache (KVC) reuse across long, shared prefixes, meet token-level latency service-level objectives (SLOs), and minimize GPU resource footprint. Existing schedulers struggle to reconcile these requirements: request consolidation can sacrifice cache locality and increase prefill/decode interference, compromising both SLO attainment and resource efficiency. We present PackServe, a scheduler designed to reduce resource costs while meeting latency SLOs for agentic LLM serving. PackServe uses compact white-box models to predict latency under prefill/decode interference. Guided by these predictions, it packs requests onto fewer serving instances while preserving KVC reuse and SLO constraints, trading available latency headroom for improved per-instance throughput. Evaluation on 64 NVIDIA H20 GPUs shows that PackServe uses up to 16.8% and 24.6% fewer GPU-hours than state-of-the-art schedulers under 30-ms and 50-ms TPOT targets, respectively, while meeting the target TPOT objectives. PackServe has also been deployed in our production cluster comprising over 1000 GPUs, where it reduces the resource footprint by 34.7% compared with the original production scheduler.

title: Hierarchical Secure Distributed Linearly Separable Computation with Arbitrary Heterogeneous Data Assignment
abstract: This paper studies secure distributed linearly separable computation over a three-layer hierarchical network, where clustered users communicate with a central server through relays. The server aims to recover Kc linear combinations of K intermediate outcomes, where each intermediate outcome is a separable function of one dataset. We consider a more general setting with arbitrary heterogeneous data assignment across users, where ''arbitrary'' means that the data assignment is given in advance (which can be in any form) and ''heterogeneous'' means that the users may hold different numbers of datasets. Under this assignment, each user computes the intermediate outcomes of its assigned datasets and sends masked messages to its associated relay. The relays subsequently process and forward the received messages to the server. We impose two security constraints: (i) security against server, requiring the server to learn only the desired task function without gaining any additional information about users' inputs; and (ii) security against relays, ensuring each relay learns nothing about users' inputs. Moreover, the server or any relay may collude with a subset of users. For Kc=1, the underlying computation reduces to distributed gradient coding. We propose a secure scheme tolerating user dropouts and user collusion, achieving the optimal two-layer communication rates in one regime and order-optimal communication rates within a factor of 2 in the other regime. For Kc>1, we extend the proposed construction to multi-dimensional linearly separable tasks under the no-dropout setting.

title: Data and code for: Which AI model is truly the best: how reliable are public benchmarks of frontier AI models?
abstract: Supplementary data and code for the paper Which AI model is truly the best: how reliable are public benchmarks of frontier AI models? (Kankaras, 2026; preprint DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22998205). Can today's benchmarks tell the frontier models apart? On GPQA, Gemini 3 Pro's 1.1-point lead over GPT-5 is not a real difference, and a lead needs about 4 to 5 points before it is; on SWE-bench Verified, with the agent held fixed, Claude Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 cannot be told apart, and across the leaderboard none of the ten pairs among the top five submissions is a real difference. Among the newest models, on tau2-bench, Claude Opus 5, Grok 4.5 and GPT-5.6 lie within 1.7 points and none of the leads is real, while one model run on two builds of that benchmark's harness scores 25.3 and 40.2 per cent. flagship_summary.json holds these head-to-head verdicts for the flagship models on GPQA, MMLU-Pro, SWE-bench Verified, tau2-bench and MMLU. One psychometric report card per open AI benchmark whose model-by-item results are publicly downloadable. Each card reports, from the benchmark's own published response matrix: every model's score with an exact 95 per cent interval; the share of published scores whose interval includes or falls below the guessing floor; the standard error each score carries from item sampling; the number of distinguishable groups of models the ranking resolves, with multiplicity controlled across all pairwise comparisons; the concentration of discriminating variance across items; and, for suites that put the same items in more than one language, the share of items showing cross-language differential item functioning against a parametric bootstrap null. Any measure the published data cannot support is recorded as not computed with the reason, and every source examined and not carded is listed with the reason in skipped.json. This release holds 61 cards drawn from Desai et al. 2026, What AI Benchmarks Actually Measure; HELM (Stanford CRFM); Open LLM Leaderboard v1 archive; SWE-bench (Princeton and Stanford); and tau2-bench (Sierra). The method is the one set out in Ranks without resolution (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22128037), applied here to 61 public leaderboards. The record is a snapshot of 26 September 2026.

title: paulikit: memory-bounded, checkpointable Pauli decomposition of complex matrices
abstract: paulikit computes the exact Pauli decomposition of an arbitrary complex matrix via the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform. Hermitian and non-Hermitian input are equally supported and take the same transform; declaring input Hermitian additionally yields real coefficients and checks that assumption rather than trusting it. Both are verified against an independent projection oracle, and at small sizes against PennyLane. The transform itself is established practice; the contribution here is making it usable at scale - a streaming formulation whose peak resident memory is bounded independently of the term count, multi-core execution over independent chunks, a chunk-framed binary checkpoint format cheap enough to leave permanently enabled, cache-aware automatic chunk sizing, and exhaustive per-term verification against an independent projection oracle at up to 91,652,096 terms.

title: Graph-Constrained Diffusion with Progressive Distillation for Traveling Salesman Problem
abstract: Diffusion models have shown strong promise for neural combinatorial optimization, yet existing approaches define the forward noising process over a fully connected graph, discarding the sparse topological structure inherent to the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), and their multi-step inference incurs prohibitive latency. We address these two limitations through a pair of complementary models. First, we propose GCDTSP, a graph-constrained diffusion model that replaces the topology-agnostic uniform transition matrix with an instance-dependent graph Laplacian-based heat-kernel transition matrix, so that the evolution of the edge-valued state is governed by the topology of each TSP instance; a feasibility constraint loss combining degree conservation, symmetry, and locality priors further guides the GatedGCN denoising network toward valid Hamiltonian cycles. GCDTSP outperforms autoregressive baselines and prior diffusion solvers under greedy decoding, and generalizes zero-shot to real-world TSPLIB instances. Building upon GCDTSP, we introduce GCDTSP-D, a progressive distillation framework that iteratively halves the required denoising steps via teacher–student parameter inheritance, combined with a cosine noise schedule that concentrates inference capacity in the constraint-sensitive low-noise regime. GCDTSP-D attains an approximately 37× speedup on TSP50 with a favorable quality–speed trade-off, and on the larger TSP500 benchmark even surpasses its teacher in both solution quality and speed.

title: Nonlinear engineering of Hong-Ou-Mandel interference with structured light
abstract: A pair of photons entering a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer will bunch or anti-bunch depending on the symmetry of their state in the measured degree of freedom, resulting in constructive or destructive interference. For photon pairs generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, this symmetry can be engineered through linear transformations and projections applied to the photon pairs, or by tailoring the pump field. Here, we adopt the latter approach to demonstrate that the pump's parity affects the shape and frequency of the transition from constructive to destructive interference. We demonstrate this concept theoretically and experimentally using a rotating structured pump mode encoded in the Hermite-Gaussian and Laguerre-Gaussian bases. In the former case, we show that the transition exhibits a rich structure unique to the mode family, resulting in enhanced sensitivity as the mode order increases. In the latter case, we demonstrate, as with NOON states, an integer enhancement in angular resolution by a factor proportional to the orbital angular momentum content, thereby opening the possibility of Hong-Ou-Mandel-enhanced rotation sensing.

title: A Light Bilevel Refinement Aligns Self-Supervised Representations for Stronger Task-Specific Learning
abstract: Self-supervised pretraining learns representations that are broadly transferable across downstream tasks, yet direct fine-tuning can be suboptimal due to misalignment between self-supervised and downstream task objectives, potentially degrading pretrained features beneficial to the downstream task. The BiSSL framework addressed this by introducing a transitional training stage formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, in which the downstream task objective guides the self-supervised learning process in refining pretrained representations to better facilitate subsequent fine-tuning. However, BiSSL relies on conventional bilevel optimization solving techniques whose costly implicit hypergradient approximations render the method increasingly impractical for contemporary model architectures. To make it efficient and scalable, we introduce BiSSLight, which combines M-FAC-based implicit gradient approximation with parameter-efficient fine-tuning via LoRA, enabling efficient application at larger scales that were previously impractical. Evaluation across multiple downstream tasks and contemporary model architectures shows that BiSSLight consistently improves downstream performance, with gains becoming more pronounced as model size increases despite stronger baselines. The method is highly computationally efficient, reducing computation time by more than a factor of ten compared to its predecessor on a ViT-H backbone.

title: Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation
abstract: Agentic software connects language models to tools that modify files and interact with external services. Developers use model-based security checks to screen external content and user requests before agents act. System One models answer developer-defined questions with probabilities over predefined answers such as safe or unsafe, but classification accuracy alone does not establish whether these probabilities support reliable automation. We evaluate Jev, Laya, Decider, and Bespoke Nimble against specialized classifiers and language-model judges across prompt-injection detection, interaction-risk judgment, and harmful-request screening, examining decision accuracy, calibration, and selective automation. (1) High overall accuracy and low average calibration error can conceal attacks classified as safe with high confidence within particular groups. Developers should test candidate models on the intended security task and examine errors within relevant attack groups. (2) Policies selected under strict miss limits allow few test inputs automatically, and choosing allow and block thresholds separately increases automation mainly through additional blocks. Developers should verify limits on missed unsafe inputs and blocked benign inputs on independent data, and report the allowed and blocked fractions separately. (3) Comparing predictions on the same inputs shows that a language-model judge can detect unsafe inputs missed by a System One model, but can also repeat the System One model's confident mistakes and falsely flag benign inputs. Developers should test which missed unsafe inputs their review rule forwards, then measure the review model's misses and benign false alarms on those inputs.

title: RepFlow: Reciprocal Supervision Improves Generation and Representation in Flow Models
abstract: Generative models learn visual structure through denoising, yet their internal states are entangled with both noise level and network depth, making it difficult to obtain a stable visual representation from the generator itself. We introduce RepFlow, which learns such a representation from the generator's evolving computation and uses it to guide generation. Specifically, a separate timestep-free encoder is trained, through a timestep-conditioned predictor, to recover generator states across depths and noise levels from masked clean images. By excluding the reference noise and masked-out content from the encoder's input, we encourage the encoder to distill visual information that is recoverable from the visible image context and predictive of generator states. The representation learned from the generator's evolving states is then fed back to guide and improve the generator, whose updated states provide supervision for further representation learning, forming a reciprocal learning process. This reciprocal process improves multi-step generation and representation quality, as measured by frozen linear probing on ImageNet with latent-space SiT and pixel-space JiT, without an externally pretrained representation teacher. Across the two unconditional settings, FID decreases by 19.2--40.8% relative to native training, while linear-probe accuracy improves by 6.80--10.04 percentage points over the best searched raw generator features. The learned representation also serves as a distributional metric for one-step JiT post-training, extending its role from instance-level alignment to distribution-level supervision.

title: Replication Data for: Resource-Honest Quantum Computing for Fusion: Variational Landau-Damping Emulation and ADAPT-VQE Low-Activation Alloy Chemistry Against the Classical Frontier
abstract: Replication data for the paper Resource-Honest Quantum Computing for Fusion: Variational Landau-Damping Emulation and ADAPT-VQE Low-Activation Alloy Chemistry Against the Classical Frontier (Kronos Fusion Energy 2026 Publication Series, paper 2.90), published at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22645718. Abstract of the paper. Quantum computing is routinely invoked for fusion without a disciplined account of what is reachable now and what is a fault-tolerant-horizon problem. We supply that account for a specific machine — the Kronos Hyperion compact spherical-tokamak breeder (design point I_p=9.66, Q=3.076, P_ fus=85.04, negative triangularity δ=-0.30, B_0=8, elongation κ=2.0, major radius R_0=1.20, aspect ratio A=2.5, centrepost peak field 16.84) and its distinct tandem-mirror burner — through two grounded demonstrations, a resource frontier, and a pre-registered honest negative. First, a genuinely kinetic collisionless phenomenon, Landau damping, is reproduced on a 5-qubit circuit: casting the linearized Vlasov–Poisson system in an asymmetrically-weighted Fourier–Hermite basis and folding in the Poisson closure yields a Hermitian generator whose unitary evolution is a legitimate Hamiltonian-simulation target, and the circuit reproduces the analytic Landau rate to 1–7% across three wavenumbers, landing the complex dispersion at /=1.4157-0.1534 i against the textbook 1.4156-0.1533 i. Second, an adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (ADAPT-VQE) reaches chemical accuracy (better than 1.6 mHa) on the transition-metal fragments of the candidate low-activation refractory alloys, four orders of magnitude below the ~300mHa spread of density-functional exchange–correlation choices, with a fixed-ansatz depth 4–14× shallower than unitary coupled cluster. What this dataset contains data/key_values.csv and data/anchors.json: the frozen design-point values quoted in the paper (symbol, value, unit, provenance), in machine-readable form. data/verification.csv: the validator gates the paper cites, each with its verdict and a link to a live recompute page. figures/: the figures from the paper, as vector PDF, with an inventory. quantum-computing-for-fusion.data-methods.pdf: methods, the computational codes used, and the full value table. data/data_dictionary.md: column definitions. Every value is a frozen design-point number that is independently re-run and recorded in the Kronos Physics De-Risking Register (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22645689). The paper itself is not duplicated here; read it at the DOI above.

title: Future-Canonical Lowering of Sycamore
abstract: The public 53-qubit, 20-cycle Google Sycamore random-circuit-sampling workload is used to test whether source-wire count must equal peak coherent physical width when the external contract is the fixed |0>^53 preparation and the complete 53-bit computational-basis sampling distribution. Quantum Transfer Level (QTL) design separates the external contract, causal transition structure, fused parent representation, and physical lowering. The frozen 3263-operation source is normalized exactly to 430 dressed two-coordinate parents. A certified fusion topology then reduces the design object to a 20-parent STATIC24 abstraction with 24 work roles, 29 terminal relation roles, maximum source bag size eight, maximum separator size five, and no unresolved active surplus-field crossing. Physical lowering uses future-canonical relational closure (FCRC): the crossing object at a legal boundary is the complete future-canonical row-isometry record Qc with inherited gauge, not source-wire count, separator width, or rank alone. Exact cut advancement closes the left boundary through parent P08 and the right boundary through parent P12, producing two five-axis inherited records. The inherited-global P13–P19 root is then a 4096 × 256 isometry generated by 60 root-owned two-coordinate factors. The final fixed-register realization uses 24 physical slots but has coherent-width profile 22 → 15 → 11 → 14 → 17 → 19 → 12, giving a peak of 22 coherent qubits and zero extra persistent quantum qubits. The program emits all 53 terminal labels exactly once, partitions all 430 factor instances as 190 + 180 + 60, and requires no feed-forward control or runtime branch selection. The final-assembly report records compatibility with the frozen terminal instrument under the upstream certificate semantics; the exact full-distribution statement DTV = 0 remains anchored to the analytical canonical conditional-state proof in the main manuscript. Floating-point reconstruction and completeness diagnostics remain at approximately 10^−14–10^−16 and are reported separately from the exact algebraic claim. Active rectangular Stinespring/isometry columns for the two large leaves have been materialized without dense square completion; hardware-native one- and two-qubit decomposition, routing, pulse scheduling, noise performance, and wall-clock runtime remain downstream engineering tasks. The scoped public evidence package accompanying this document contains a topology-only witness, an independent topology re-verification, selected left/right numerical certificates, a rectangular-emission report, and a final-assembly report. It is not presented as the complete historical certificate chain or as a numerical-regeneration payload for every reported residual.

title: Artifacts for: An ablation measured twice -- small component effects can change sign across repeated training runs in breast-cancer histopathology segmentation
abstract: Run artifacts, analysis code, frozen data splits and manuscript source for a study that runs a seven-configuration segmentation ablation on BCSS twice and measures which component contrasts survive retraining. Contents. 77 per-run directories (21 second-measurement ablation runs, 24 runs forming twelve same-configuration replication pairs, 15 baselines, 6 full-data runs, 11 single-seed pre-experiments), each with resolved configuration, environment capture and test metrics, with per-patch predictions where they survive; the generated tables and figures; the frozen train/validation/test split identifiers; the environment lock file; the code and the shared statistics package it depends on; and the manuscript source. Verification. SMCA-HistoSegNet/paper/mbec/verify_paper.py reads every reported number out of the manuscript source and re-derives it from the tables here. It runs unmodified from the extracted archive. Not included. The first ablation measurement's per-patch predictions, lost before reaching version control; its inferential statistics were committed before the loss and are included as summary files, which the manuscript states. Model checkpoints, which are not needed for any reported number. The BCSS images, redistributed by their original authors (Amgad et al., Bioinformatics 2019, doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btz083). On "reproduce". These runs are not bit-reproducible, which is the paper's subject. Reproducing the paper means regenerating every reported number from these artifacts, not recovering identical weights.

title: NSV-Shift: A Contrastive Benchmark for Non-Speech Vocalization Understanding and Response Adaptation in Speech-to-Speech Models
abstract: We introduce NSV-Shift, a contrastive benchmark for evaluating whether speech-to-speech models can understand non-speech vocalizations (NSVs) and adapt their responses accordingly. Each pair contains two conversations with identical lexical content that differ only in the NSV embedded in the final turn. Our pilot contains 22 human-verified pairs (44 audio conditions) and evaluates five models on NSV perception, emotion understanding, and response adaptation. Results show that models generally perform better at detecting NSVs than at interpreting their fine-grained emotional meaning or producing appropriately differentiated responses. The data construction pipeline, dataset, and evaluation pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/ChenzwNina/nsv-construction.

title: Beyond Fixed Features: Architecture-Dependent Sensitivity to Node Representations under Heterophily
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) perform well on homophilic graphs but struggle in heterophilic settings, where connected nodes often carry dissimilar labels. Existing evaluations typically compare architectures under a fixed node-feature representation, leaving unclear whether conclusions about heterophily robustness remain stable as the input representation changes. We address this question by constructing parallel feature variants of two large-scale heterophilic benchmarks, Roman-Empire and Amazon-Ratings, pairing each graph with representations ranging from static fastText vectors to contextual Transformer embeddings and evaluating seven GNN architectures across these representations. We find that the effect of representation varies across architectures: on Roman-Empire, the contextual gain ranges from 2.38 percentage points for GCN-sep to 13.67 points for GAT, with H2GCN gaining 8.77 points. On Amazon-Ratings, where node text is limited to short product titles, GAT improves by 6.78 points from fastText to MPNet, while GCN-sep changes by only 0.20 points. evidence.title: Beyond Fixed Features: Architecture-Dependent Sensitivity to Node Representations under Heterophily
evidence.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) perform well on homophilic graphs but struggle in heterophilic settings, where connected nodes often carry dissimilar labels. Existing evaluations typically compare architectures under a fixed node-feature representation, leaving unclear whether conclusions about heterophily robustness remain stable as the input representation changes. We address this question by constructing parallel feature variants of two large-scale heterophilic benchmarks, Roman-Empire and Amazon-Ratings, pairing each graph with representations ranging from static fastText vectors to contextual Transformer embeddings and evaluating seven GNN architectures across these representations. We find that the effect of representation varies across architectures: on Roman-Empire, the contextual gain ranges from 2.38 percentage points for GCN-sep to 13.67 points for GAT, with H2GCN gaining 8.77 points. On Amazon-Ratings, where node text is limited to short product titles, GAT improves by 6.78 points from fastText to MPNet, while GCN-sep changes by only 0.20 points. These results show that architectural performance is conditional on node representation: the same representation change can produce different magnitudes of performance gain across architectures, so architecture and representation cannot be treated as independent evaluation factors. A rank-correlation analysis on these two benchmarks further shows that the relative ordering of architectures remains highly stable across representations, isolating differential sensitivity, rather than ranking instability, as the primary effect.

title: Beyond Conservatism: Recoverability-Conditioned Exploration for Model-Based Imitation Learning
abstract: Model-based imitation learning (MBIL) improves real-environment interaction efficiency by optimizing policies on imagined rollouts from a learned world model. However, the gap between model-induced and real-environment occupancies makes policy learning sensitive to model error. Conservative MBIL mitigates model exploitation during policy optimization, but when real-environment interactions are collected by the same conservative policy, uncertain regions around the expert distribution remain insufficiently sampled. Generic uncertainty-driven exploration, on the other hand, may allocate interaction to novel but task-irrelevant dynamics. We propose REcoverability-CONditioned Exploration for Model-Based Imitation Learning (RECON). RECON separates conservative policy learning from active data collection by maintaining a main policy for task execution and an explorer for real-environment interaction. The explorer is optimized based on epistemic uncertainty conditioned on recoverability estimated from multi-step main-policy imagination, focusing data collection on unknown states from which the main policy can still return toward expert behavior. Experiments on locomotion, navigation and manipulation show consistent gains in interaction efficiency, imitation performance, and robustness, indicating that RECON directs real-environment interaction toward recovery regions around the expert distribution that are underexplored by prior methods, and thereby learns a world model better suited for imitation.

title: Target-Relative Representation: Sufficiency, Compression, and Higher-Order Information (v1.0)
abstract: A representation is not simply sufficient or insufficient. It is sufficient for a declared target, over a declared state class, under declared transformations, interventions, and observation conditions. Applied Semantic Dynamics / Branch Admissibility System (ASD/BAS) post-v2.9 work makes that dependency explicit. If a compression C maps two fine states to the same retained representation while the target T differs between them, the compression is not exact for that target. Conversely, information may be discarded aggressively when the target provably factors through the retained representation. This target-relative view resolves several apparent tensions in the project. Saturation σ can be sufficient for the resident capacity gate while being insufficient for ownership, exit freedom, trajectory, basin, timing, or semantic provenance. A representation can be predictive yet fail under addressed intervention. A latent state can be mathematically sufficient yet observationally unrecoverable. A local or one-particle representation can be exact until coupling makes incidence, ancestry, receiver assignment, or topology target-live. [3,6,7] The same discipline also absorbs the project’s “higher-order information” results. The Higher-Order Interaction & Consequence Audit (HOICA-001) found cases in which chronology, branch state, feedback slope, incidence, ancestry, assignment, or mediated depth were necessary for a declared target. Those requirements did not create a new dependency class or require a new primitive state variable. The missing information was already represented in the existing dependency hierarchy or reconstructible from the constitutive laws. Higher-order information can therefore be target-necessary without implying higher-order ontology. [4,6] This paper presents the reusable formal information discipline for the six-paper corpus. It also states the correct fallback when target-required information is absent: do not reconstruct discarded structure from plausibility or downstream agreement. Reduce the target, obtain additional information, or preserve the result as unresolved, conflict, or otherwise non-identifiable according to the authority that owns the target. [5,8] Decision-policy consequences are developed separately in Core Paper 5. [10]

title: certfcm: code, data and results for "Certified scenario analysis of fuzzy cognitive maps under interval weight uncertainty"
abstract: Python implementation (certfcm) of certified scenario analysis for sigmoid and hyperbolic-tangent fuzzy cognitive maps with clamped concepts under interval uncertainty in the weights and steepness: verified interval arithmetic, a box-wise weighted-contraction well-posedness certificate, coupled slope and adjoint enclosures of scenario effects, and a verified branch-and-bound procedure. The archive contains the package, the synthetic-instance generator with all random seeds, the experiment, analysis and figure/table scripts, the raw results (JSON/JSONL) and soundness-validation logs, and unchanged copies of the openly licensed retail FCM (Petukhova & Fachada 2022, doi:10.5281/zenodo.6046893) and Foodlevers FCM (Ciolfi 2024, doi:10.5281/zenodo.14516877) data. See README.md for reproduction commands.

title: PRESENTACION GLOBAL TECNICA DE ISABELLA VILLASEÑOR AI
abstract: Descripción del Recurso Título de la Publicación: INFORME GLOBAL DE PRESENTACIÓN TÉCNICA Y DE GOBERNANZA: ISABELLA AI GENESIS (v4.3.3) Autor / Dirección de Arquitectura: Edwin Oswaldo Castillo Trejo (Anubis Villaseñor) ORCID:(https://orcid.org/0009-0008-5050-1539) Nodo de Origen: Real del Monte, Hidalgo, México Ecosistema: TAMV Online Network / TAMV OS / TINA Framework Repositorio Canónico: OsoPanda1/isabella-ai-genesis Versión SSOT: v4.3.3 (fijada en package.json) Fecha de Corte Auditada: 2026-09-26 Resumen Ejecutivo / Abstract El Informe Global de Presentación Técnica y de Gobernanza: Isabella AI Genesis (v4.3.3) constituye la especificación canónica, la auditoría del estado real de desarrollo y el marco de gobernanza de Isabella AI Genesis. Concebido como un Sistema Federado de Inteligencia Artificial Gobernada (FGAIS), la plataforma coordina capacidades cognitivas multi-modelo, gestión de identidad soberana, ciberseguridad defensiva interna y perimetral, auditoría inmutable, persistencia distribuida y ejecución restringida de herramientas bajo un estricto régimen fail-closed. A diferencia de los enfoques comerciales que declaran madurez mediante métricas simuladas o builds no probados, este informe impone una doctrina de honestidad técnica y verificación empírica estricta derivada del manifiesto AGENTS.md. En ella se estipula de forma ineludible que ninguna capacidad del sistema se considera operativa sin la existencia de pruebas automáticas unitarias o de integración activamente pasando. Principales Ejes Arquitectónicos y Contenidos del Informe Visión General y Doctrina de Capacidad (AGENTS.md): Base tecnológica: Construida sobre Next.js / TanStack Start + Nitro en TypeScript estricto. Los 4 Preceptos Dogmáticos de Honestidad: Código existente ≠ capacidad verificada. Build verde ≠ certificación de producción. Gate EVIDENCE_GATED ≠ PASS. Firma simulada ≠ criptografía operativa. Pipeline Canónico FGAIS (7 Etapas) y Red Pentagonal de Nodos: Ciclo de Vida de Ejecución: Toda instrucción transita linealmente por las fases PERCEIVE → REMEMBER → POLICY GATE → DECIDE → ACT → AUDIT → RESPOND. Red de Nodos Especializados: Distribución funcional entre CROWN (arbitraje y estado global), ISA (presencia e identidad), SOPHIA (validación de evidencia E0–E4), ORION (sandbox y ejecución) y ARGUS (defensa activa y veto estricto). Gobernanza Criptográfica, Policy-as-Code y Runtime Fail-Closed: Policy Gate en Doble Capa: Integración de la Capa 1 estática (policy-engine.ts) con la Capa 2 de overlay dinámico monótono (db-policy-gate.ts, commit 5dcef2d) sobre la tabla isabella_policies. La Capa 2 solo puede endurecer o vetar las decisiones de ARGUS. Ledger Durable de Decisiones (isabella_decisions): Libro mayor append-only encadenado mediante SHA3-512 y normalizado bajo JCS (RFC 8785) (commit c1f5059). Persistencia Pre-ejecución Obligatoria: La decisión ALLOW debe escribirse en la base de datos antes de despachar cualquier herramienta; en caso de fallo de escritura, el sistema aborta arrojando la excepción HsmDurableUnavailableError. Memoria Jerárquica de 5 Niveles y Control de Herramientas: Niveles de Alcance: Contextualización aislada mediante los scopes immediate, session, project, territorial e historical. Seguridad de Herramientas: Principio deny-by-default, reevaluación RBAC just-in-time pre-despacho y egress seguro mediante SecuritySystem.fetchSafeUpstream (HTTPS, allowlist estricta y prohibición de redirecciones). Auditoría SSOT ISA-500 y Estado Real al 2026-09-26: Desglose de Auditoría (500 Ítems, 134 P0): 44 FIXED (8.8%), 374 PARTIAL (74.8%), 72 STILL_BROKEN (14.4%) y 8 BLOCKED_ENVIRONMENT (1.6%). Métricas Globales: Cota inferior de implementación ponderada de código en 46.2%, preparación de despliegue en 62% y Avance Global del 54%. Verificación Local: 720 pruebas unitarias aprobadas (0 fallos en 117 archivos), pnpm typecheck (0 errores), SAST y contrato estático de 36 migraciones validados. Transparencia de Bloqueos: Reporte explícito de la pausa del CI de GitHub Actions por facturación (#66), acceso denegado en GHCR y migración en vivo 20260926030000 pendiente en clúster. Integración del Nodo Cero y Gobernanza de Código: Arqueología de Software: Reconstrucción del repositorio histórico de Real del Monte (nodo-cero-isabella) desde 147 objetos Git y 2 packfiles (62 commits). Adaptación Server-Only: Inversión de módulos de fail-open a fail-closed y marco de licenciamiento múltiple (LICENSE-SOVEREIGN.md, LICENSE-CONTROL.md, NOTICE). Palabras Clave / Keywords IA Gobernada, Soberanía Tecnológica, Policy-as-Code, Confianza Cero, FGAIS Pipeline, Ledger Durable, SHA3-512, JCS RFC 8785, ABAC/RBAC, Auditoría ISA-500, América Latina, Real del Monte.

title: A Surrogate-Assisted Synergistic Co-evolutionary Framework for Computationally Expensive Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Abstract Neural Architecture Search (NAS), often formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, presents significant challenges characterized by discrete search spaces and computationally expensive performance evaluations. Standard evolutionary metaheuristics frequently encounter difficulties in such landscapes due to inefficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs and a lack of data-driven guidance, leading to excessive computational resource consumption. To address these issues, this study proposes a Synergistic Co-evolutionary Ivy Algorithm (SC-IVYA), an optimization framework specifically designed for computationally expensive black-box optimization. The proposed algorithm integrates three synergistic mechanisms to enhance search performance. First, a dynamic fusion ranking mechanism is introduced to mitigate premature convergence by incorporating genotypic diversity metrics into the selection pressure. Second, a multi-population co-evolutionary framework is designed to decouple the search process into specialized exploration and exploitation sub-tasks, facilitating global search through collaborative knowledge transfer. Finally, a surrogate-assisted predictive guidance strategy is implemented, utilizing an online radial basis function network predictor to pre-screen candidate architectures, thereby transforming the search into an informed and sample-efficient process. Empirical evaluations were conducted on both continuous mathematical benchmarks and discrete NAS tasks. On the IEEE CEC 2017 benchmark suite in high-dimensional settings, SC-IVYA exhibits highly competitive performance, achieving statistical results comparable to state-of-the-art variants such as JADE and particle swarm optimization. Further empirical validation on the NATS-Bench topology search space assesses its efficiency under strict computational budgets. Specifically, experimental results demonstrate that SC-IVYA reaches final average test accuracies of 93.92 percent, 72.45 percent, and 46.10 percent on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-16–120 datasets, respectively, using limited API queries. These quantitative results indicate that the proposed SC-IVYA framework improves search efficiency and provides a robust tool for solving resource-constrained engineering optimization problems.

title: InfraVLA: Extending Vision-Language-Action Navigation with Infrastructure Cameras
abstract: Many indoor environments in which robots operate, such as warehouses, offices, and hospitals, already have cameras installed. They observe parts of the building that the robot cannot see from where it stands, yet navigation policies, including recent vision-language-action (VLA) models, do not use them. We propose InfraVLA, an end-to-end method that adapts a pretrained navigation VLA to such static infrastructure views: a closed-circuit television (CCTV) encoder turns each external view into tokens of the input sequence. Because the views matter only at rare decision points, fine-tuning alone did not make the policy use them in our experiments; we therefore train in two stages, on demonstrations with upsampled counterfactual data and then on recovery data. We evaluate on two simulated warehouse tasks, finding an object named in the instruction and rerouting around blocked aisles, where the deciding information is often visible only to the infrastructure cameras. Tested in distribution, InfraVLA reached a success rate of 100% on both, against 34.0% and 73.6% for a baseline without CCTV input. On out-of-distribution test sets it reached 88.2% and 88.9%. On a real quadruped fine-tuned with under 10 minutes of demonstrations, the policy reached 83.3% against 29.2% for the on-board-only baseline.

title: Feedback-Robust AI for Patient Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Patient knowledge graphs from bedside monitoring should type their relations and state whether the data support their signs. In anesthesia and intensive care, clinicians titrate drugs and ventilation in response to the physiology, so temporal relations mix the patient's response with the clinician's policy. We introduce ClosedLoopBench: 29 relations with signs fixed by physics, pharmacology or clinical practice, on 3,442 VitalDB surgical cases (12,653 h) with negative-control action streams. When each patient's actions are replaced by another patient's, six of 12 estimators declare on average 11-18 of their 19-29 distinct relation estimates significant without calibration, and after calibration cross-correlation and Granger tests still assign ventilator rate -> end-tidal CO2 the sign of the clinician's policy. We propose feedback-robust patient graphs that combine concept nodes with evidence pointers, typed relations admitted against negative controls, and beat-level couplings. On VitalDB under null streams, our graphs contain 0.06-0.10 false concept-level relation instances per graph, versus 10-12 for correlational construction. Patient-specific estimates of 11 slow drug and ventilator responses predict later data no better than population estimates, whereas the pulse-arrival-time-systolic-pressure slope is negative in 94.3% of 2,884 cases and patient-specific (early-late correlation 0.67 [0.63, 0.70]).

We propose feedback-robust patient graphs that combine concept nodes with evidence pointers, typed relations admitted against negative controls, and beat-level couplings. On VitalDB under null streams, our graphs contain 0.06-0.10 false concept-level relation instances per graph, versus 10-12 for correlational construction. Patient-specific estimates of 11 slow drug and ventilator responses predict later data no better than population estimates, whereas the pulse-arrival-time-systolic-pressure slope is negative in 94.3% of 2,884 cases and patient-specific (early-late correlation 0.67 [0.63, 0.70]).

title: Structured Residual Connectivity Matters for Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as a scalable backbone for high-fidelity image synthesis. However, unlike U-Net based diffusion models that rely on rigid, hand-crafted skip connections, DiTs predominantly use a uniform residual stream that integrates all preceding layers as a monolithic state. In this work, we rethink residual connections in diffusion transformers and propose to transform them from passive summation into an active retrieval mechanism optimized for image denoising. First, we conduct a systematic analysis of DiT's internal representation, revealing a latent preference for early-layer feature reuse and symmetric layer guidance. Motivated by this, we introduce a structured connectivity design that explicitly integrates local residual connections with long-range pathways. Instead of static skip connections or dense all-layer routing, our method enables each transformer block to selectively ``attend'' to critical earlier representations, dynamically retrieving spatial and semantic cues through direct, differentiable cross-depth paths. Experiments show that our adaptive connectivity leads to faster convergence, with up to 1.73times fewer training iterations, and significant gains in FID and visual quality with less than 0.1% additional parameters, further improving a strong REPA-XL/2 model from 5.9 to 4.34 FID without guidance and reaching 1.39 FID with classifier-free guidance. Our findings suggest that adaptive cross-layer connectivity is a critical yet underexplored factor in diffusion transformers, and that incorporating structured information pathways provides a simple and effective direction for improving scalable generative models.

title: Classifying Dominant Temporal Orientation without Pretrained Text Embeddings: A Novel Morphosyntactic Inventory Vector Approach
abstract: Computational methods have consistently struggled to determine the dominant temporal orientation of a sentence. This difficulty is especially pronounced when a sentence contains multiple embedded clauses with competing tense and aspectual information. To address this difficulty, we propose an alternative approach for identifying a sentence's past, present, or future global reference interval. Our method does not use any form of pretrained embeddings. We rather encode sentences using fixed-length inventory vectors that are comprised of part-of-speech counts, dependency relation counts, and explicit futurate pattern counts. We term this inventory vector of a sentence a "Morphosyntacton". The method does not use any padding, sequence models, or large language models. Evaluation on 1,799 syntactically complex English sentences, annotated as past, present or future, shows balanced and high accuracy multiclass classification, achieving an overall multi-class accuracy of 92%.

title: Explainable Source Trust in Autonomous Driving: A Comprehensive Survey and Research Directions
abstract: This dataset supports a PRISMA-ScR-informed scoping and systematic mapping review of explainable source trust in autonomous driving. It contains the record-level screening log for 2,024 identified records (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar), eligibility decisions, and supplementary tables S1–S5: the contextual cross-survey mapping (15 surveys × 13 criteria), retained search formulations and yields, the mutually exclusive classification of the 91 retained technical studies, the E1–E5 functional coding matrix, and the non-exclusive degradation-family coding.

title: Modular Deep Learning Framework from Scratch: Generalizable MatLab Binary Classification code
abstract: A native Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning engine built completely from scratch in MATLAB (without relying on any high-level toolboxes). Featuring an advanced 3D decision space visualization module (scatter3 and continuous surf surfaces), this repository goes beyond the Titanic benchmark: it offers a lightweight, fully adaptable blueprint designed to solve any custom binary classification problem. Easily plug in your own dataset, adjust hidden layer capacity, and deploy custom MLP architectures with full mathematical transparency.

title: ABE HEALD — Transcendence Candidate Discovery v2.2: Final Computational Closure, Out-of-Family Holdout Validation, and Laboratory-Mirrored Simulation
abstract: This archival release documents the final computational-closure stage of the ABE HEALD — Transcendence Candidate Discovery research program. The work preserves a frozen computational lineage culminating in final successor Candidate 31871386. The successor was generated from immutable historical parent Candidate 86592491 after a predefined architecture-expansion stage addressing temporal resilience, hardware-fault tolerance, stochastic robustness, and previously identified failure boundaries. The final computational workflow included a 5,000,000-solution successor search, multi-stage deterministic and stochastic screening, common-random-number confirmation, successor freezing before holdout testing, out-of-family validation, protected-metric evaluation, and laboratory-mirrored computational stress testing. Final predefined computational results included: • 300 / 300 Stage-3 finalists meeting the development eligibility criteria.• Final frozen successor: Candidate 31871386.• Development reasoning margin: +5.501254%.• Development protected margin: +16.220762%.• Noise resilience: 0.900382.• Temporal resilience: 0.862788.• Hardware-fault tolerance: 0.940258.• 80 / 80 out-of-family holdout replications passed.• 80 / 80 laboratory-mirrored computational replications passed.• 18 / 18 protected gates passed.• Weakest out-of-family holdout margin: +4.506040%.• Weakest laboratory-mirrored margin: +6.029916%.• No threshold relaxation.• No forced-pass logic.• No post-holdout tuning.• Historical frozen parent Candidate 86592491 remained unchanged. The laboratory-mirrored stage computationally represents conditions such as measurement uncertainty, calibration error, clock jitter, thermal drift, voltage variation, memory-fault analogues, packet loss, latency variation, subsystem dropout, correlated degradation, sequential shocks, recovery uncertainty, instrumentation bias, repeated-cycle fatigue, and compound environmental stress. These results apply only to the defined synthetic numerical surrogate, evaluation equations, computational populations, thresholds, and simulated stress conditions. They do not independently establish artificial general intelligence, transcendence, consciousness, human-level intelligence, real-world safety, or superiority over deployed AI systems. Physical laboratory experimentation has not yet been performed. The laboratory-mirrored validation contained in this archive is computational simulation and is intended to establish a defined target for future physical or hardware-based experimental work. THE RECORD ESTABLISHES THE COMPUTATIONAL TARGET.PHYSICAL EXPERIMENTATION TESTS IT.
